rv.q: This is a performance of hypnotic authority.

"Shatteringly good Broadway revival...A great production of Eugene O’Neill’s monumental drama requires a towering performance in the crucial role of Hickey, and Washington memorably delivers one...Happily, the cast assembled by the veteran director George C. Wolfe is almost without a weak link...
The great strength of Washington's work is its intimacy.
You want to talk theater? Take that, people!
The cumulative effect of this handsomely decrepit production is bracing.
So best to simply relish the power of a great play and the actors — all the actors — who tell the story.
In those closing scenes, the play finally achieves its full tragic grandeur.
Washington’s below-surface intensity caught so effectively by the camera is of little use here, and there are moments when he overcompensates with a forced bigness at odds with his cast mates
Here, the punches are sometimes packed and sometimes pulled.
It leaves the audience on ice, waiting for Washington and this production to fully come alive in the last act.
Wolfe’s revival feels full of untackled problems, unmet challenges, and untapped dramatic energy.
Wolfe and Washington and a marvelous cast demonstrate that the play is indeed a monumental piece of theater.
Wolfe achieves with actors what other fine directors this Broadway season do with turntables, wires, elevators, and dry-ice fog.
Washington, in his fifth Broadway appearance in 30 years, proves once again to be as dynamic a performer on stage as he is on screen, perhaps even more so.
Fortunately with George C. Wolfe and his superlative company to guide us through, we've got a match made in theatre heaven.
When that secret is revealed, Washington’s Hickey proves a transfixing storyteller, a salesman who knows how to close.
Even at four hours, you won't want to miss this one, either.
Everyone shines in this production.
In Wolfe’s hands every performance on the stage of the Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre is a world unto itself – a nihilistic one at that.
Washington makes the sequence intimate, suspenseful, and powerfully poignant.
His performance overall is the finest piece of stage work I’ve seen from him since he first riveted Off

Nevertheless, the production succeeds largely on account of a terrific ensemble (which also includes Frank Wood, Bill Irwin, Michael Potts, Tammy Blanchard and Austin Butler) in great character roles.

The trimming manages to direct more attention to the individual denizens of Harry Hope’s saloon, each with a story to tell, each story giving another talented performer a chance to shine. Colm Meaney is bar owner Harry, blustery but non-judgmental to the point of being kind.
It’s an awkward problem that casts a shadow of confusion over this otherwise self-assured production.
Washington has shiny star quality and 100-proof charisma that fits like a glove for Hickey.
That doesn't quite happen here.

In this Broadway production, the carousing and confessions, the lost lives and thwarted ambitions, the sense of a world against you and of you pitted against the world, somehow never pierces as hard as it should.
He takes the glad-handing aspect of Hickey too literally so it is difficult to understand his sway over the denizens of Harry Hope’s saloon.

While the larger vision and the major performance lack distinction, the pleasures of this revival of The Iceman Cometh are derived from seeing the members of the ensemble bring to life the people with whom O’Neill once shared his drinks and despair.
But their current incarnations fall short of their full, devastating potential.

"The only truly great thing about George C. Wolfe’s mostly traditional production is that the (color-blind) casting of superstar Denzel Washington in the lead role of glad-handing salesman Theodore 'Hickey' Hickman will likely introduce this play to a whole new cadre of theater lovers.
A couple like Mr. Irwin and Mr. Potts manage to rise above the general cacophony, but a dreary sameness creeps in all the same and leaves us by the end in a Novocain stupor.

Because what happens over the next four hours (two intermissions and one short break) is a solidly contracted dance towards death, filled with engaging and deep performances from a cast of pros relishing and finding humor in every morsel and whiskey shot.
Wolfe is one of the A-est of A-list theater directors today, and he has given us a production to remember.
The entire cast, under the energetic direction of Wolfe, simmers and stews, drinks and dreams, brilliantly.
This is one of O'Neill's major works, and it is rewarding to see it performed anew, especially with Washington making his bid to make the renowned role his own.
Even so, The Iceman Cometh, and Denzel Washington, are treasures not to be missed and a fine look at alcoholism, and America, in 1912.
Here he constructs a symphony from O'Neill's lyrical text, aided with no doubt the strongest ensemble cast on Broadway.
Washington’s magnetism cannot force us to feel that feeling, and if it doesn’t exactly leave us ice cold, it’s no more satisfying than watery gin.
Now that this great actor has stuck his pick into it, I suggest it’s time for others to put The Iceman Cometh on Broadway ice for a couple of decades before once more taking up the tongs.
Denzel Washington and David Morse provide solid performances and manage to make this ponderous evening bearable.

cn.t: Washington leads a strong ensemble in Wolfe's energetic revival of O'Neill's masterwork, though opinions split on whether the production fully captures the play's bleak depths beneath its unexpectedly vibrant surface.

sg.ra: Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs orchestra floor is raked and the house has a single balcony (not two), so Center Orchestra rows A-D get close detail without the second-balcony crush. Playbill's Outsiders guide names Orchestra C Row B Seat 112 the best seat in the house; SeatPlan and Headout both call rows A-D the premium pick for plays specifically. Row numbering 101-114 (center block) means 107/108 sit dead-center on the aisle.

Multiple guides single out Center Orchestra rows F-K as the Jacobs value play: same centered sightline as the A-D premium block, but priced well below because Row I is where the mezzanine overhang line starts (overhead, not yet cutting into the stage). The Jacobs' single-balcony design and raked orchestra floor keep these rows clear, and Wikipedia notes two columns at the rear-of-orchestra promenade supporting the balcony - those sit behind Row N/O, so F-N stay clear of the columns.

SeatPlan and Headout both say the mezzanine overhang 'cuts into the top of the stage' starting at Row O - this is the Jacobs' specific geometry (mezz front at Row I, stage-top cutoff at Row O). Wikipedia adds that the rear-orchestra promenade has two columns supporting the balcony, so patrons here also share space with structural posts. Wheelchair spaces are assigned to rows I, J, P, and R per Headout, confirming P/R are flat promenade rows.

sg.vl: Fine if you pick single-digit seats
sg.ra: Side orchestra uses odd 1-27 (Left) and even 2-28 (Right). SeatPlan notes sightline restrictions intensify at double-digit seats (far aisle) and in back rows. Playbill's Outsiders guide specifically flagged that the right-side front rows were 'a clearer view' than left, because the show's tire set piece on house-left obstructs Orchestra L front rows - this is show-dependent but illustrates the Jacobs' shallow thrust style where side props block near side-orch seats. An AVFMS Orchestra G17 reviewer wrote 'sometimes the boxes block your view of the jungle gym' - the side boxes eat into side-orch sightlines.

sg.vl: Sharp angle, sells as obstructed for a reason
sg.ra: The Jacobs has 2 box seats on each side (16 total per Wikipedia) elevated beside the orchestra. TripAdvisor's theatre rep confirmed obstructed-view seats cluster 'on the extreme sides of the front mezzanine and orchestra' - the boxes are the prime example. Multiple guides warn boxes 'cut off high center stage scenes' and block views of stage-left from the right box / stage-right from the left box. SeatPlan explicitly recommends left boxes over right because the right box loses more stage-left content.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, 9 rows from stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Mezz rows A-B the best mezz view in the Jacobs; an AVFMS reviewer at Mezz A107 wrote 'you are perfectly centered and at only nine rows from the stage' - the Jacobs' single-balcony design (per Wikipedia, no second balcony) means the mezz sits close rather than stacked high. Row B dodges Row A's safety-bar issue that SeatPlan calls 'obstructive to shorter patrons.' Front mezz is 168 seats in rows A-D with premium centered sightlines on the full set.

sg.vl: Row E is the legroom hack
sg.ra: Rear mezz is 252 seats in rows E-K. The Jacobs-specific quirk: Row E sits directly behind the front-mezz cross-aisle with a curtain/bannister (not a wall), giving 'extra space' for taller patrons per SeatPlan - Playbill's Outsiders guide confirms Mezz Left Row E has 'a curtained divider between the aisle and row' for extra legroom. Rows G-K are flagged as value seats because the mezz has a 'good rake' and Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs has only one balcony so even Row K stays surprisingly close. An AVFMS Mezz H22 reviewer noted 'legroom is not great' - stick to Row E or aisle seats.
